newsitem.title: PERU: Rebels say Peru obstructs negotiated end to crisis.
newsitem.headline: Rebels say Peru obstructs negotiated end to crisis.

text.p: Marxist rebels holding 72 hostages at the Japanese ambassador's residence accused the Peruvian government on Monday of obstructing talks for a peaceful solution to the 111-day siege.

The Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) hostage-takers told Reuters there was no chance of resuming direct talks -- on hold for three weeks -- until the government showed the "political will" to address their demand for the release of jailed comrades.

"The only thing the government is doing is putting obstacles in the way," rebel leader Nestor Cerpa Cartolini said in an interview by walkie-talkie from within the besieged compound. "So long as our demands are not listened to, we are not leaving the residence."
"To have direct talks there has to be something concrete -- a political will for an accord," Cerpa added.

The MRTA's position added to pessimism that the two sides were far from returning to the negotiating table despite energetic shuttle diplomacy by a three-man guarantors' panel striving to hammer out an agenda for fresh talks.
President Alberto Fujimori said late on Sunday face-to-face talks would remain on hold until he was confident negotiations would bring real progress.

"(Government negotiator Domingo) Palermo cannot go and bash heads with the MRTA, but rather (talk) in an environment in which we can say that we are making progress," Fujimori said in an interview with Peru's Panamericana television network.

With no visible progress in Latin America's longest-ever hostage siege, Peru's Congressional President Victor Joy Way asked Tokyo on Monday to be patient in waiting for a peaceful solution to the standoff.

"We must not set deadlines which will put pressure on ourselves. Impatience is our worst enemy in this process," Joy Way told local radio station Radioprogramas del Peru in an interview from Tokyo. The legislator was visiting Japan to meet Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto.

A group of about 20 heavily armed MRTA rebels stormed a cocktail party thrown by Japanese Ambassador Morihisa Aoki on Dec. 17 and took more than 500 guests hostage. They released most of the hostages, but kept a group including Aoki, two Cabinet ministers, Fujimori's brother, the Bolivian ambassador and two dozen Japanese businessmen and diplomats.
Fujimori reiterated the government's pledge not to use force to end the 15-week standoff "unless there is an uncontrollable situation, in which there is a victim."
Cerpa claimed regular medical check-ups by doctors entering the diplomatic mansion ensured the remaining captives had no serious health problems.
"The situation is not serious, there is a controlled situation," the rebel leader said.
There has been no sign that the MRTA has harmed any of the hostages, although many are reported to be suffering stress-related disorders after months in captivity.

"My father suffers from (high) blood pressure and has a heart problem, too, so we have always been worried about his health," Ana Teresa Pantoja, daughter of captive former Supreme Court President Moises Pantoja, told the America Television network.
